strengths: The framework addresses a relevant problem: constructing discrete EEG representations from individual channels. Combining raw waveforms with localized spectral features is well motivated, and separating tokenization from downstream classification offers useful modularity.

The evaluation covers four datasets and reports means and standard deviations over five seeds. Results consistently favor the proposed model, with particularly encouraging improvements on IIIC: balanced accuracy increases from the strongest baseline’s 0.5421 to 0.5775.

The appendix includes useful ablations of input domains, positional embeddings, vocabulary size, masking strategies, and encoder pretraining. Architecture, optimization, STFT settings, and dataset splits are documented in considerable detail.

Replacing LaBraM’s tokenizer improves its reported performance on both evaluated datasets, providing evidence that the tokenizer can benefit another architecture. Retrieval experiments and motif visualizations also extend the evaluation beyond classification.
weaknesses: The central benefit of discretization is not isolated. The method combines established STFT processing, vector quantization, transformers, and masked prediction, but lacks a matched continuous version using the same encoders and training budget. Consequently, gains could arise from the architecture or spectral inputs rather than discrete tokens. Moreover, Section 4.1 incorrectly distinguishes its patchwise quantization from conventional image VQ, which also quantizes embedding vectors at individual spatial locations.

The frequency-preservation analysis in Section 5.3 is not technically convincing. The numerical representation used for the Fourier transform of token sequences is unspecified. If token IDs are used, spectral entropy changes under arbitrary codebook relabeling despite identical representations. Even for embeddings, higher temporal spectral entropy does not establish preservation of the original EEG frequency content and can reflect noise. Direct frequency-band reconstruction or controlled signal experiments are needed.

The generalization and channel-flexibility claims exceed the experiments. Appendix B.1 states that the tokenizer and encoder are pretrained separately within each dataset. There is no evaluation transferring a fixed tokenizer across datasets, acquisition systems, or channel configurations, nor an evaluation on the motivating one- or two-channel tasks. Integration into LaBraM demonstrates compatibility, but does not establish these broader capabilities.

The masked reconstruction objective admits an unaddressed shortcut: Section 4.1 supplies the complete raw waveform alongside the masked spectrogram, while reconstructing an STFT deterministically obtainable from that waveform. Thus, successful reconstruction need not demonstrate the claimed learning of missing temporal or cross-frequency dependencies. An aligned raw-input masking control would help establish what the objective contributes.

Several headline improvements are uncertain relative to training variability. On TUEV, balanced accuracy is 0.4943 ± 0.0516 versus 0.4682 ± 0.0856 for LaBraM and 0.4898 ± 0.0105 for the raw-only variant; paired uncertainty estimates are absent. The CHB-MIT test set contains only two subjects. Additionally, the controlled single-dataset retraining regime supports comparisons within that setting, rather than unqualified superiority over pretrained foundation models, and comparable baseline tuning budgets are not documented.

The token-quality evidence is overinterpreted. Using only 9.78% of the vocabulary on TUEV could indicate redundancy reduction or codebook underutilization; utilization alone cannot distinguish these. Class-exclusive token counts depend on sample frequency and dataset composition, while the selected motif examples do not establish general physiological interpretability or robustness. The retrieval protocol also omits subset sizes and explicit handling of self-matches and samples from the same subject.

Despite extensive hyperparameter tables, important reproduction details remain missing, including the codebook and commitment loss weights, EMA update settings, and definitive masking rates. The manuscript also provides no implementation link. These omissions particularly hinder verification of the tokenizer and its diagnostic analyses.

The appendix provides substantial ablations covering input domains, masking strategies, positional embeddings, vocabulary size, downstream depth, and pretraining. Cross-dataset transfer and token retrieval experiments add useful evidence.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not adequately isolated. The framework combines established spectral processing, transformers, vector quantization, and masked prediction, but lacks a matched continuous-latent baseline without quantization or a comparison using LaBraM tokens as inputs to the same downstream model. Consequently, the results do not establish whether discrete tokenization itself provides the benefit over the encoder architecture and training procedure.

The frequency-learning analysis in Appendix C.1 is technically unconvincing. Applying a DFT to token IDs produces statistics that change under arbitrary codebook relabeling. If embeddings are used instead, their representation and aggregation must be specified. In either case, higher token-sequence spectral entropy does not establish better recovery of physiological EEG frequencies. Low codebook utilization and selected waveform examples also do not establish meaningful, robust motif discovery.

The masking objective permits an unexplained shortcut. Figure 2 masks the spectrogram while showing an unmasked raw-signal branch, although the spectrogram is deterministically derived from that signal. Thus, supposedly hidden information remains available through the other branch. The paper should clarify masking across both inputs and reconcile its masked-reconstruction description with a loss summed over all time-frequency locations.

Performance and generality claims exceed the comparisons. On IIIC, the highlighted 36% improvement is against a weak pretrained baseline, while vanilla BIOT already achieves 0.4932 kappa versus the proposed 0.4979. On multi-dataset CHB-MIT, balanced accuracy decreases from BIOT’s 0.7068 to 0.6471. Comparable baseline tuning budgets are not documented. Additionally, the LaBraM integration replaces prediction targets, so it does not validate the advertised use of discrete tokens as downstream inputs.

Cross-device evidence remains preliminary: EESM23 uses only two test subjects, one device dataset, and supervised target-task fine-tuning. Variation across training seeds does not quantify uncertainty across subjects. A strong sleep-staging baseline, a training-from-scratch control, and broader subject-level evaluation are needed to substantiate device-agnostic transfer.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The supplied PDF has blank code and checkpoint links, and important settings such as masking ratios, reconstruction/codebook loss weights, and EMA decay are unspecified. These omissions make the methodological ambiguities difficult to resolve independently.

strengths: The reusable single-channel vocabulary addresses a relevant EEG representation problem. Separating tokenization from multichannel modeling provides a plausible route to supporting different electrode configurations.
Some reported gains are substantial: multi-dataset TUEV Cohen’s kappa improves from 0.5273 for the strongest listed baseline to 0.6189, with a compact 1.9M-parameter system.

The experimental effort is considerable: four clinical benchmarks, ear-EEG transfer, five-seed reporting, integrations with BIOT and LaBraM, and ablations covering input domains, masking, vocabulary size, positional embeddings, and downstream depth. Appendix C.3 also provides encouraging frozen-tokenizer transfer results.
weaknesses: The central benefit of discrete tokenization is not isolated. There is no matched continuous-feature baseline using the same encoders and downstream architecture, nor a comparison that feeds an existing neural tokenizer’s codes into the same classifier. Consequently, the gains could arise from the encoder, training procedure, or tuning rather than the discrete motif vocabulary.

The masking objective has an apparent information shortcut. Figure 2 shows spectrogram masking while the corresponding raw EEG remains available through the temporal branch. Since the reconstruction target is computed from that signal, successful reconstruction need not require inferring missing information from context. The paper should clarify masking across both branches and compare against ordinary unmasked autoencoding before attributing gains to its proposed masking mechanism.

The frequency-learning analysis in Appendix C.1 does not establish its claimed conclusion. Spectral entropy of a token sequence is not evidence of coverage of physical EEG frequency bands; if computed on token IDs, it also changes under arbitrary codebook relabeling. Low codebook utilization and class-exclusive tokens likewise require controls for codebook collapse, token rarity, and class frequency before supporting physiological interpretability.

Several headline improvements depend on weak reproduced baselines. For example, the reported 36% IIIC kappa gain compares against multi-dataset LaBraM at 0.3658, whereas vanilla BIOT already achieves 0.4932 versus the proposed method’s 0.4979. Extensive tuning is described for the proposed system, but comparable baseline tuning budgets are not established. This limits confidence in the magnitude and attribution of the improvements.

The foundation-model integration claims need qualification. LaBraM uses the proposed tokenizer to generate pretraining targets, which does not demonstrate the central claim of reusable discrete inference inputs. Improvements also involve tradeoffs: Table 9 shows multi-dataset BIOT’s CHB-MIT balanced accuracy falling from 0.7068 to 0.6197. The table contains improvements in 31 of 36 comparisons, approximately 86%, rather than the stated 93%.

Cross-device generalization remains preliminary. EESM23 uses supervised adaptation and a single split with only two held-out test subjects. Variation across five training seeds does not measure uncertainty across subjects or devices, and the reported significance tests are insufficiently specified. Broader subject-level evaluation is needed to support the scalability claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful architecture tables. The supplied manuscript leaves the promised code and checkpoint links blank and omits important settings, including masking proportions, reconstruction/codebook loss weights, and codebook EMA parameters. These omissions make the unresolved implementation questions harder to verify.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: reusable EEG representations that accommodate different channel configurations. The single-channel tokenizer and separate downstream model provide a practical modular design.
Reports substantial improvements on TUEV: multi-dataset pretraining achieves Cohen’s kappa of 0.6189 versus 0.5273 for BIOT, with improvements in balanced accuracy and weighted F1.

The evaluation covers four clinical EEG benchmarks and ear-EEG sleep staging, reports five-seed variability, and includes ablations of input domains, masking, positional embeddings, vocabulary size, and downstream depth.
Cross-dataset transfer results and improvements when integrating with BIOT and LaBraM provide encouraging evidence that the learned representations have utility beyond the proposed classifier.
weaknesses: The central benefit of discrete tokenization is insufficiently isolated. The method combines established vector quantization, dual-domain encoding, and masked reconstruction, but lacks a matched continuous-representation baseline using the same encoder, downstream architecture, and training budget. The existing ablations therefore cannot establish whether quantization drives the gains.

Some headline improvements depend on unexpectedly weak pretrained baselines. On IIIC, the claimed 36% kappa improvement compares 0.4979 against 0.3658, while unpretrained vanilla BIOT already achieves 0.4932. The substantial degradation after baseline pretraining needs investigation and comparable tuning documentation. Superiority is also not consistent across metrics: multi-dataset CHB-MIT balanced accuracy is 0.6471 versus BIOT’s 0.7068.

The masking objective has an unresolved reconstruction shortcut. Figure 2 and Section 3.2 mask the spectrogram while apparently retaining the corresponding raw signal in the temporal branch. Since the spectrogram is determined by that signal, reconstruction need not require recovering missing information from context. Coordinated masking across both branches should be clarified and evaluated.

The frequency-learning analysis in Appendix C.1 does not substantiate its interpretation. Fourier analysis of categorical token IDs changes under arbitrary codebook renumbering; if embeddings are analyzed instead, this is unspecified. Moreover, token-sequence spectral entropy does not directly measure preservation of EEG frequency content. Low codebook utilization and a few selected waveform examples also provide limited evidence of physiologically meaningful motifs.

The LaBraM integration does not demonstrate the advertised use of discrete tokens as downstream inputs: Section 4.3 replaces its tokenizer during masked pretraining, apparently retaining its role as a prediction target. This supports improved pretraining targets but only partially supports the broader reusable-input-interface claim.

Device generalization is demonstrated on one ear-EEG dataset with supervised adaptation and only two held-out test subjects. Without repeated subject splits or a comparable model trained from scratch, the evidence cannot establish broad device independence or isolate the benefit of transferred tokenization. Five training seeds do not capture uncertainty across subjects.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite detailed architecture tables. The announced code and checkpoint links are blank in the supplied manuscript, and masking rates, reconstruction/codebook loss weights, EMA settings, and the statistical procedures underlying significance claims are not specified.
